strengths: The paper provides genuinely novel exact (non-asymptotic) characterizations of the variance and NSR of the REINFORCE estimator for structured control problems (one-step and multi-step LQG, polynomial dynamics with polynomial feedback), derived via careful Gaussian moment calculus (Wick/Isserlis theorem) and lifted-dynamics representations. This is a substantial technical contribution that goes well beyond prior variance bounds (e.g., Preiss et al., Zhao et al.) by giving exact expressions rather than asymptotic or loose bounds.

Theorem 4 offers a clean, rigorous bridge from a local variance lower-bound condition (~1/sigma^2) to a formal 'escape from a fixed ball' guarantee for SGD, giving a concrete mathematical mechanism connecting variance blow-up to training instability, rather than just empirical correlation.

The central empirical/theoretical finding -- that NSR is highly non-uniform and typically increases sharply as policies approach optimality because optimal policies tend toward determinism (Corollary 7, Σ→0) -- is an interesting and non-obvious insight with a clear causal story, and is corroborated across several different system classes (LQG, quadratic/cubic polynomial systems, LQR/pendulum with MLP policies, and even MuJoCo Hopper/HalfCheetah).

Extensive and carefully documented experiments (main text and appendix) show consistent qualitative trends across many system types and optimizers (GD/SGD/Adam), including a targeted ablation (Figure 7) isolating statistical noise as the cause of policy collapse, and a useful demonstration that naive Monte Carlo estimation of variance/NSR is unreliable relative to the exact computation, justifying the value of the theoretical machinery.

The discussion section thoughtfully extends the core analysis qualitatively to baselines/actor-critic and entropy regularization, acknowledging both their mitigating effects and their limitations (fragility of baseline cancellation, need for accurate value approximation), showing good awareness of the work's scope and limitations.
weaknesses: The most 'exact' and clean results (Theorem 3, closed-form NSR) are limited to very simple one-step or simplified isotropic settings; the fully general multi-step LQG result (Theorem 6) is an extremely complex multi-term decomposition (six terms for K, four for ℓ, each with further sub-expansions) that is 'exact' only in the sense of being numerically evaluable, and provides limited direct interpretability -- the paper falls back on a looser upper bound (Theorem 8) to extract intuitive scaling laws, somewhat undercutting the stated advantage of exactness over bounds.

For the most practically relevant setting (nonlinear dynamics with neural policies), only an upper bound is given (Theorem 11), and the accompanying experiments (Figure 6, MuJoCo Figure 10) rely on Monte Carlo estimation of NSR/variance -- the same estimation approach the paper itself demonstrates (Appendix B, Figure 9) to be unreliable at capturing trends. This creates some tension: the paper's core selling point is exactness, yet the generalization to realistic nonlinear/neural settings must resort to the very estimation method shown to be inadequate.

The work is purely diagnostic/explanatory; no new algorithm, variance-reduction technique, or mitigation strategy is proposed or empirically validated. The discussion of baselines and entropy regularization as remedies is qualitative and not tested experimentally, leaving the practical actionability of the findings underdeveloped for a paper whose framing emphasizes implications for training instability.

Polynomial-system extension (Section 3) has combinatorial/exponential complexity in horizon, dimension, and degree, restricting experiments to very small horizons (T=6, T=3) and low-dimensional toy dynamics; it is unclear how far these findings extrapolate to realistic polynomial or higher-dimensional systems.

Theorem 4's escape-from-ball guarantee is stated for a scalar SGD recursion on σ with a stylized noise-variance lower bound condition; its formal connection to the actual multi-parameter (K, ℓ) SGD/Adam dynamics studied in the experiments is only heuristic/qualitative, not directly established.

The paper is dense with heavy notation and many results are relegated to lengthy appendices (35 pages), which, combined with the narrow scope of exact results (linear/polynomial systems under Gaussian exploration), may limit the broader applicability and accessibility of the contribution to the wider RL community working with more complex policies and environments.

strengths: The paper provides genuinely exact (non-asymptotic) closed-form or algorithmically computable characterizations of REINFORCE variance/NSR for finite-horizon LQG systems (Theorems 3, 6, 8) and polynomial systems with polynomial feedback (Proposition 10), going beyond prior work (e.g., Preiss et al. 2019, Zhao et al. 2011) that only provided variance bounds rather than exact expressions.

The theoretical results are complemented by a general variance upper bound for arbitrary nonlinear dynamics and expressive (including neural) Gaussian policies (Theorem 11), which extends the qualitative insight (inverse scaling in policy covariance, dependence on policy Jacobian) beyond the structured settings and connects it to Monte Carlo experiments on LQR/pendulum/MLP and MuJoCo Hopper/HalfCheetah.

Theorem 4 offers a formal (if simplified, scalar) mechanism linking unbounded gradient-noise growth near deterministic policies to a positive probability of 'escaping' any fixed neighborhood, giving a rigorous, if partial, bridge between the NSR blow-up phenomenon and observed training instability/policy collapse.

The empirical package is thorough and purposeful: it isolates the proposed mechanism through a controlled ablation (comparing small batch, large batch, and exact-gradient training) that convincingly shows statistical noise—not merely large learning rate or momentum—drives policy collapse (Figure 7), and it demonstrates the phenomenon's generality across double-integrator, polynomial, LQR/MLP, pendulum, and MuJoCo environments.

The discussion section honestly engages with limitations and extensions (baselines, entropy regularization, alternative policy families), providing informative, non-trivial analysis (e.g., how baseline approximation error can still leave an O(1) residual that reintroduces the blow-up) rather than merely listing caveats.
Reasonable reproducibility: explicit formulas, proofs, and experimental hyperparameters (learning rates, batch sizes, architectures) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central qualitative finding—that REINFORCE variance/NSR scales as roughly O(σ^-2) and blows up as the policy becomes near-deterministic—is largely consistent with, and to some extent already implied by, prior analyses (e.g., Zhao et al. 2011's O(σ^-2) bounds); the paper's novelty lies primarily in exactness and generality rather than in identifying a fundamentally new phenomenon, which somewhat tempers the significance of the contribution.

The exact multi-step LQG expressions (Theorem 6) are extremely intricate (six-term and four-term decompositions with many auxiliary matrices), and the paper itself falls back on a looser upper bound (Theorem 8) to extract interpretable scaling laws, suggesting the exact characterization, while mathematically complete, offers limited additional practical insight over the bound.

The analysis is restricted to the vanilla REINFORCE estimator without baselines/advantage estimation, which is rarely used in practice as-is; the paper's discussion of how baselines/entropy regularization interact with the phenomenon is qualitative and not accompanied by a rigorous exact characterization analogous to the main results, leaving the practical relevance to modern actor-critic algorithms somewhat speculative.

The polynomial-system framework's computational complexity grows combinatorially with horizon, degree, and dimension, restricting demonstrated experiments to very short horizons (T=6, T=3) and low-dimensional toy systems, limiting the scope of validated generality.

For nonlinear/neural-policy settings, the paper must rely on Monte Carlo estimation of NSR (with generous 1-minute-per-iteration budgets), yet the paper's own Appendix B experiments show Monte Carlo estimates fail to accurately track the true variance/NSR trends even with large rollout budgets—raising concern about the reliability of the nonlinear-system experiments (Figures 6, 10) that depend on such estimates.

The connection between high NSR and optimizer instability remains largely correlational for the general (non-LQG) experiments (synchronized fluctuations shown via visual inspection), and the authors explicitly acknowledge that a formal characterization of the NSR–instability relationship for realistic multi-dimensional adaptive optimizers (e.g., Adam) remains an open problem; Theorem 4 only covers a simplified scalar SGD update.

Notation is dense with numerous auxiliary matrices (Mss, Mse, Mee, U, V, etc.) across sections, which, combined with the reliance on appendix-only proofs, may hinder accessibility for readers seeking to verify or build upon the exact results without substantial effort.
